title: print() displays the current value on the screen
when_to_show: When predicting the output of `print()` or following the execution order of multi-line code
body: print() is a function that displays the value inside the parentheses on the screen. When reading code, it serves as a reference point for checking what the calculated value is up to the current line. Python code executes line by line from top to bottom, unless there are special conditional statements or loops. Therefore, if a variable’s value has changed before `print()` is called, the output will reflect the updated value. If there are quotation marks, as in `print("name")`, the string “name” is printed exactly as written; if there are no quotation marks, as in `print(name)`, the value stored in the variable `name` is retrieved and printed. When reading code, it’s helpful to check, line by line, where a concept first appears and what variables or output it leads to. Beginners often focus only on getting the final result correct and tend to overlook intermediate values, so it’s important to practice writing down the execution order line by line, even for small examples. This card focuses on developing the habit of reading code rather than simply memorizing it. This card emphasizes that `print` displays the current value on the screen, rather than relying on rote memorization. If a variable is inside a `print` statement, the value stored in that variable at that moment is printed. However, `print` itself does not store values or return function results. In output prediction problems, you must track how values changed in the lines preceding the `print` statement and count only the lines that actually appear on the screen as the result.
detail: The `print` function displays the current value inside the parentheses on the screen. It is important to note that `print` does not create a new value; rather, it displays the value that was calculated and stored before the program reached that line. If quotation marks are present, the text is printed as-is; if there are no quotation marks, the function retrieves and prints the current value stored in the variable.

title: Output prediction follows all lines preceding the `print` statement.
when_to_show: When tracking changes in variable values in a problem involving selecting output results
body: It’s easy to get the output prediction problem wrong if you solve it by looking only at the last `print` line. `print` doesn’t suddenly generate a value on that line; rather, it displays on the screen values that have already been stored and calculated in previous lines. Therefore, you must first check what values have been assigned to the variables and then trace the flow to see if those values are copied to other variables or recalculated. If a value is assigned to the same variable multiple times, the value stored last is used in subsequent lines. When reading code, it’s helpful to check, line by line, where this concept first appears and how it leads to subsequent variables or output. Beginners often focus only on getting the final result correct and tend to overlook intermediate values, so it’s important to practice writing down the execution order line by line, even for small examples. This card focuses on developing the habit of reading code rather than simple memorization. To predict the output, you must trace all the lines preceding the `print` statement. Even if a `print` statement contains only a variable, the value of that variable may have already changed due to previous assignments and calculations. When reading code, you must distinguish between the values displayed on the screen and those that have only been calculated in the meantime. It’s also important to count only the lines that are actually printed.
detail: Predicting the output isn't just a matter of looking at the last `print` line. You must track what value was assigned to the variable before the `print`, whether it was reassigned, and whether the result of the calculation changed. When reading code, make a note of the variable's current value after each line is executed, and base your judgment on the value at the time of the `print`.

title: A variable is a label used to track a value.
when_to_show: When reading code in which a value is stored in a variable or the value of the same variable is changed again
body: A variable is a name assigned to a value so that it can be referenced later. “x = 3” means that the name “x” now refers to the value 3. If you assign a new value to the same variable—such as “x = 5”—the code will use the new value, 5, from that point on. Therefore, when reading a problem involving variables, it’s safest to write down the variable’s current value on each line. A common mistake beginners make is confusing the variable name itself with the value it holds. When reading code, it’s helpful to check, line by line, where a concept first appears and what variables or output it leads to afterward. Beginners often focus only on getting the final result correct and tend to overlook intermediate values, so it’s important to practice writing down the execution order line by line, even for small examples. This card focuses on developing the habit of reading code rather than simply memorizing it. This card emphasizes that a variable is a label used to track a value. If you assign a new value to the same name, that new value is used in subsequent lines. When solving problems, it’s helpful to read the code while continuously updating the current value next to the variable name. In particular, you must check what the value is immediately before an output to predict the result displayed on the screen.
detail: A variable is a label used to track a value. If you assign a new value to a variable with the same name, the new value—not the previous one—will be used in subsequent lines. When solving problems involving variables, you should clearly distinguish between the initial value, intermediate assignments, and the final output. The key is to distinguish between the name itself and the value it refers to, and to update the current value on each line.

title: In college entrance exams, you calculate the right side and then store the result on the left.
when_to_show: When reading code that updates the value of the same variable, such as `x = x + 1`,
body: In assignment, the right-hand side is evaluated first, and the result is then stored in the variable on the left. For example, `x = x + 1` might seem strange, but the expression first reads the previous value of `x` from the right-hand side, adds 1 to it, and then stores the result back into `x`. Therefore, the value of a variable can change over time. When reading code, if the same variable name appears multiple times, you shouldn’t just remember the initial value; you must continuously update your understanding of what the new value is after each line is executed. This card is not intended merely for memorizing definitions; it serves as a supplementary explanation to help you understand how variables, data types, functions, files, and API flows are connected in actual Python code. When solving problems, first locate the line in the code where this concept appears, and then categorize that line: is it a step that reads input, changes a value, evaluates a condition, or stores or outputs a result? Doing so allows you to apply the concepts learned from short examples to reading actual project code. In an assignment, the right-hand side is evaluated first, and the result is then stored in the variable on the left. `x = x + 1` reads the existing value of `x`, adds 1 to it, and then stores the result back into `x`. If a variable is assigned a new value multiple times, the previous value is replaced by the new one. When reading code, you must continuously update the current value of each variable after each line is executed.
detail: In assignment, the right-hand side is evaluated first, and the result is then stored in the variable on the left. In `x = x + 1`, the expression reads the previous value of `x` from the right-hand side, adds 1 to it, and then stores the result back into `x`. Therefore, even for the same variable, the value may change from one line to the next. When reading code, you must keep track of the current value after each assignment.

title: If there are quotation marks, read it literally
when_to_show: When distinguishing between strings and variable names that look similar
body: In Python, a value enclosed in quotes is a string. Since a string is a literal value, "name" is a four-character string, not code that searches for the variable `name`. Conversely, "name" without quotes is interpreted as a variable name. If you write `print(name)` after `name = "Python"`, "Python" is printed, but if you write `print("name")`, the word "name" is printed. This distinction is a very common source of errors in beginner-level output prediction problems. When reading code, it’s helpful to check, line by line, where this concept first appears and what variables or output it leads to. Beginners often focus only on getting the final result correct and tend to overlook intermediate values, so it’s important to practice writing down the execution order line by line, even for small examples. This card focuses on developing the habit of reading code rather than simply memorizing it. This card emphasizes that, rather than rote memorization, you should read the text literally when quotation marks are present. '3' is the character '3', not the number 3, and 'name' is the character 'name', not the variable name. When reading code, you must distinguish between values inside quotes and variable names. If you overlook this difference, it’s easy to mispredict the results of addition, comparisons, and output.
detail: If quotation marks are present, Python interprets the contents as a literal string rather than a variable name. `print('name')` prints the text "name," but `print(name)` prints the value stored in the `name` variable. Even though it looks like a number, '3' is a string, so you must first check for the presence of quotation marks before performing any calculations.

title: String numbers and actual numbers are different.
when_to_show: When distinguishing between the results of calculations involving numbers with quotation marks and those without
body: Even though they look similar on the screen, '3' and 3 are different values. '3' is a string, and 3 is a number. When you add two strings together, it’s concatenation, not arithmetic, so '3' + '4' becomes '34'. When you add two numbers together, it’s arithmetic, so 3 + 4 equals 7. A common mistake beginners make is assuming that two values are the same just because they look the same on the screen. In code, data types are more important than how values appear. When reading code, it’s helpful to check, line by line, where this concept first appears and what variables or output it leads to afterward. Beginners often focus only on getting the final result correct and tend to overlook intermediate values, so it’s important to practice writing down the execution order line by line, even for small examples. This card focuses on developing the habit of reading code rather than simple memorization. This card emphasizes that the results for string numbers and actual numbers differ from those of simple memorization. '2' + '3' concatenates the characters to form '23', while 2 + 3 is a numerical calculation that results in 5. When reading code, you must check for the presence of quotation marks and whether any int or float conversions have occurred. Input values are often strings at the beginning.
detail: Although string numbers and actual numbers may look similar on the screen, they behave differently. '3' + '4' concatenates the characters to form '34', while 3 + 4 performs a numerical calculation and results in 7. When reading code, you must check whether values are enclosed in quotes or have been converted to `int` or `float` to accurately predict the results.

title: Basic errors often occur with names, quotation marks, and indentation.
when_to_show: When reading about common runtime errors and syntax errors in beginner-level code
body: Beginners often make mistakes in basic syntax rather than with complex algorithms. If you use a variable like `print(name)` before declaring it, you may get a `NameError`. Failing to close the quotation marks around a string can result in a SyntaxError. If the indentation is incorrect in code following a colon—such as in `if` or `for` statements—an IndentationError may occur. Error messages may look intimidating, but they usually contain hints about the line where the problem occurred or its cause. When reading code, it’s helpful to check step by step where a concept first appears and what variables or output it leads to afterward. Beginners often focus only on getting the correct result and tend to overlook intermediate values, so it’s important to practice writing down the execution order line by line, even for small examples. This card focuses on developing the habit of reading code rather than simply memorizing it. Basic errors can usually be found by following the flow of values. A NameError indicates that a name has not been defined, while a quotation mark error may mean that a string boundary has been broken. Indentation errors often occur when it’s unclear which code belongs inside a conditional statement or loop. It’s important to get into the habit of reading error messages along with their line numbers, rather than ignoring them.
detail: Beginner errors usually stem from names, quotes, or indentation. A NameError indicates that an unrecognized name was used, a SyntaxError indicates that the syntax is incorrect, and an IndentationError indicates that the indentation structure is incorrect. It’s best to read error messages starting from the last line and the line number indicated.

title: Basic grammar is the backbone of real-world code.
when_to_show: When explaining how the beginner-level grammar cards relate to actual project code,
body: Basic syntax elements—such as print, variables, strings, and numbers—aren’t just used in small examples. Real-world project code ultimately follows the same flow: storing values, calculating necessary values, and outputting the results to the screen or a file. Code that reads data files must distinguish between strings and numbers, and web app code also processes user-entered values as variables. Therefore, even though the beginner-level cards may seem like simple problems, they form the foundation for reading real-world code. When reading code, it’s helpful to check, line by line, where a concept first appears and what variables or output it leads to. Beginners often focus only on getting the correct result and end up overlooking intermediate values, so it’s essential to practice writing down the execution order line by line, even for small examples. This card focuses on developing the habit of reading code rather than simple memorization. Basic grammar is the backbone of real-world code. Basic elements such as variables, conditional statements, loops, functions, and lists come together to form file-handling and web application code. Even when faced with complex code, breaking it down into lines that store values, make decisions, loop, and produce results makes it easier to read. Viewing the fundamentals from a flow-based perspective lays a solid foundation for further learning.
detail: Basic grammar isn’t limited to simple examples—it forms the backbone of real-world code. Variables store data, strings and numbers handle input and calculations, and the `print` statement lets you verify the results. Even complex project code ultimately boils down to tracking where values come from, how they change, and where they are output.
